patch.value: pm assert: a bound over a measurement carrying polarity, scope, lifetime, enforcement level, and a required negative control, so every guarantee states which direction it can fail in

An assertion binds a measurement to a declared bound. Polarity is ceiling, floor, equals, zero, monotone_nondecreasing, monotone_nonincreasing, or subset_of, and exactly one is declared per assertion. Scope names the population the bound speaks for — active only, all statuses, or a filter expression — because a bound that is silently active-scoped always passes for the newest structural layer, which is how a governance improvement became indistinguishable from a relevance regression. Lifetime names what happens when the owning item reaches a terminal status: hold keeps comparing, retire stops and must record why the property stopped mattering. Enforcement level is block, warn, or observe, so a project adopts a bound by first watching it. A negative control is mandatory and must prove failure in every direction the polarity admits, which for a floor means both an undercut and a spurious pass. The owner is a typed relationship to the pm item that owns the property, not a string, so assertions participate in the graph and an item's blast radius includes the guarantees that depend on it. Tightening is automatic and monotone; loosening is refused unless a linked Decision item authorises it, which is what makes a repair and an erosion structurally different acts rather than the same hand edit.

An assertion declares exactly one polarity, is refused when it declares none or several, and names its measurement by id; Scope is explicit and a bound that would silently cover only active items must say so, with the population size reported alongside the observed value; Lifetime defaults to hold, retire requires a recorded reason, and an out-of-domain lifetime fails rather than falling back to the default; Automatic tightening is monotone in the good direction; any loosening is refused unless a Decision item is linked, and the refusal names the missing decision; Each assertion carries a negative control that fails in every direction its polarity admits, and an assertion whose control has never failed is reported as unproven
